title: C Exercises
description: Try one small task at a time. Read the answer notes to learn why each answer works. Use the setup lesson to run code on your computer.

exercises.question: Which tool turns C source code into a program your computer can run?
exercises.explanation: A compiler translates C source code into machine code. You then run the program it made.

exercises.question: Fill the gap: gcc hello.c ___ hello names the output program hello.
exercises.explanation: The -o flag chooses the output file name. On Windows, hello.exe is a useful name.

exercises.question: Why does this statement fail to compile?
exercises.explanation: Most C statements end with a semicolon. Write int pencils = 4; to finish this statement.
options: It needs a semicolon at the end

exercises.question: Swap the values of a and b. Use a third box, called temp, to hold one value.
exercises.explanation: If you write a = b first without saving a, the old value of a is lost. temp keeps it safe during the swap.
checklist: Keep the old value of a in temp.

exercises.question: What does this C program print?
exercises.explanation: Both values are whole numbers, so integer division drops the fractional part.

exercises.question: The C language promises that int is exactly four bytes on every computer.
exercises.explanation: C sets minimum ranges, but sizes can differ. Use sizeof to ask for the size on your computer.

exercises.question: Which numbers are printed?
exercises.explanation: The loop starts at 0. It stops when i reaches 3 because i < 3 is then false.

exercises.question: Print 1 to 15. Use Fizz for multiples of 3, Buzz for multiples of 5, and FizzBuzz for both.
exercises.explanation: The % sign gives a remainder. A remainder of zero means the number divides evenly.

exercises.question: What should appear before a call to a function defined later in the file?
exercises.explanation: A declaration tells the compiler how the function is called. For example: int add(int a, int b);
options: A declaration with its return type and inputs

exercises.question: Write average to return the mean of two whole numbers as a double. Test it with 3 and 4.
exercises.explanation: The mean is the sum divided by two. Using double keeps the half instead of dropping it.

exercises.question: Which positions are valid in an array with three items?
exercises.explanation: Array positions start at zero. The last valid position is one less than the item count.

exercises.question: What numbers are printed?
exercises.explanation: strlen counts the three letters. The array also stores a zero byte that marks the end of the string.

exercises.question: Fill the gap: int* place = ___score; stores the address of score.
exercises.explanation: The & operator gets the address of a variable. A pointer stores that address.

exercises.question: If p points to a struct, p___score reads its score field.
exercises.explanation: The arrow operator reaches a field through a pointer. With an ordinary struct variable, use a dot.

exercises.question: Make space for three int values with malloc. Check the result, store 7 in the first place, print it, then free the space.
exercises.explanation: malloc asks for memory and may fail. free gives the memory back when you are finished.
checklist: Call free once after the last use.

exercises.question: Count lines in notes.txt. Count a last line even if it has no newline at the end.
exercises.explanation: Each newline ends a line. A nonempty last piece also counts as a line, even when it has no final newline.
checklist: Close the file and handle a last line without a newline.

exercises.question: An include guard starts with #ifndef and #define, then ends with ___.
exercises.explanation: The guard lets a header body appear once even when several files include it.

exercises.question: Which action is safe for int numbers[3] = {4, 5, 6};?
exercises.explanation: Position 2 is inside this array. Positions 3 and -1 are outside it and must not be read.
